I worked on designing and implementing the Stripe Provider Microservice using Spring Boot.

Designed REST API POST /v1/checkout/sessions for creating Stripe Checkout Sessions.
Understood API versioning, request contracts, and resource management.
Explored Stripe PSP integration using Spring RestClient.
Learned the importance of separating functional logic from infrastructure concerns.
Designed a layered approach using CheckoutSessionService, StripeClient, and 
HttpServiceEngine.
Explored centralized handling of logging, authentication, timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers.
Implemented controller-to-service-to-client flow using constructor injection.
Explored Stripe CLI for webhook simulation and testing.

💡 Key Takeaway: A well-designed microservice should follow the Single Responsibility 
Principle, ensuring clean architecture, reusability, and easier maintenance.

Approving an AI system for production is not the same as governing it while it operates.

The Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority's 2026 survey highlights the difference.

94% of responding firms reported AI policies, principles, or standards. More than 90% reported pre-deployment data-risk controls such as human approval, review, and vendor due diligence. But only around half reported ongoing monitoring, leakage testing, and periodic review. Fewer than half reported incident-management and response playbooks.

What I find interesting is the contrast between governance that approves a use case and governance that remains effective after deployment.

I think of something as ordinary as hiring a pool service. We spend time researching providers, agreeing on what should be done, and signing a contract. Once the service starts, we tend to assume everything is being done as promised.

But the contract describes what should happen. It doesn't tell us what actually happened.

A launch approval works similarly. It reflects what an organization understood and tested at a particular point in time. But production behavior can change as models, data, tools, permissions, and business processes evolve.

Once AI agents begin acting, governance becomes an ongoing operational responsibility. Someone must know what agents are authorized to do, observe what actually happens, detect deviations, and have the authority and ability to intervene. Escalation and recovery procedures need to be tested, not simply documented.

In my view, the real test of AI governance is whether business and technology owners can demonstrate that the controls approved before deployment continue to work as intended, even as the environment changes.

For banks, that means connecting AI governance to the same day-to-day disciplines used to operate critical services: clear business ownership, security controls, monitoring, incident response, and independent assurance.

The goal isn't broad autonomy everywhere. It's being able to delegate the right work, at the right level of autonomy, with confidence that controls continue to operate effectively.

With a pool service, we may discover that something isn't being done only when the water turns green. With autonomous agents operating in critical enterprise systems, we need to know much sooner.

For those operating AI agents in production, how are you verifying that the controls approved at launch remain effective? What has been the hardest part of making that happen?

Work Experience in Crypto & DeFi - The Hard Truths

Market is tougher than ever, and I think the more you know about the other side of the hiring stream, the better. Here's one that everyone hiring talks about constantly, but candidates never seem to be aware of:


➡️ Stop leveraging on experience from 2+ years ago.


Sounds crazy right? Why wouldn't what I achieved 2 years ago be relevant now? 😮


The answer is simple. You work in one of the fastest paced, constantly evolving industries on earth. The market-neutral strategy that saved your firm in 2024 will tank an existing firm today. The influencers/KOL's you sourced for that DEX in 2022 don't have the same relevance in 2026. The core onchain infra codebase you wrote in 2021 doesn't apply to the AI-native coding world of today.


🚀BD outreach and partnerships? Expired.
🚀Marketing strategies that scaled users from 0-500k? Played out.
🚀Secure smart contracts that protected 6 figures? Now vulnerable.


Always lead with what you've done recently, why it was a success, and what impact you've had on the current market. If it wasn't a success, lead with what you would've done differently and how it would've changed impact.

If that aligns, then you can start walking back through previous successes and how they've led you to the point you're at now.

Onchain projects don't make hires based on legacy achievements. DeFi as we know it has been through a complete transformation in the last 18 months alone.

We need to see how you've handled it.

The Indian technology workforce may be changing not only in what people do — but in how they are employed.
CIEL HR reports that contract staffing in India’s technology sector grew 10.1% in FY26, compared with just 2.3% growth in permanent technology employment.
The shift is particularly visible in specialised areas such as AI, machine learning and cybersecurity.
And in India’s GCC ecosystem, contractual roles could represent nearly 25% of positions by the end of 2026, compared with around 15% in previous years.
There is a clear business logic.
Companies need specialised talent quickly.
Some capabilities may only be required for specific projects.
Technology requirements can change faster than traditional hiring structures.
But if flexible staffing moves from being a temporary solution to becoming a permanent part of workforce design, then we also need to think more seriously about the quality of those jobs.
For workers, a good contract role should not simply mean:
“Here is the project. See you when it ends.”
The conversation should include:
fair and transparent compensation,
reasonable notice periods,
health and other benefits,
paid leave,
clarity on contract renewal,
access to learning,
recognition of experience,
and pathways into permanent roles where appropriate.
There is nothing inherently wrong with contract work.
But there is a difference between flexibility and precarity.
And as businesses increasingly build blended workforces of permanent and contract talent, that distinction will matter more.
If contract workers are increasingly doing core technology work, should they also receive more of the protections and opportunities associated with permanent employment?

Everyone wants to build more. Fewer organisations are asking whether they have enough engineers to do it.

Over the last 12 months, I've spoken with a lot of technology leaders who have ambitious plans around modernisation, cloud adoption, AI and new product development.

The roadmap is usually clear.

The challenge is finding the people capable of delivering it.

I'm seeing organisations compete for the same skill sets time and time again:
→ Senior Software Engineers
→ .NET and Java Developers
→ Solution Architects
→ Cloud Engineers
→ DevOps Engineers
→ Data Engineers
→ AI Specialists

The reality is that demand for experienced software engineering talent continues to outpace supply in many areas.

As a result, projects get delayed, hiring processes take longer than expected, and teams end up stretched while trying to maintain delivery commitments.

The businesses that seem to navigate this best aren't waiting until a project kicks off to think about talent.

They're building relationships early, mapping future capability needs and understanding where they may need support from contract or consultancy partners.

A simple question worth asking is:

If your most important project started tomorrow, do you already know where the people are coming from?

If the answer isn't clear, it might be worth having that conversation now rather than six months from now when everyone else is hiring for the same skills.

I'm always interested to hear what challenges technology leaders are facing when it comes to software engineering hiring, team growth and project delivery.
Feel free to reach out if you'd like to compare notes on the market or discuss upcoming requirements.

To agencies replacing junior hires with AI:
Who will replace your seniors in 5 years?

I’m seeing this shift firsthand in digital marketing.

Experienced profiles are increasingly expected to use AI to handle execution faster, reducing the need to hire juniors.

On paper, it makes sense: 
Smaller teams. Lower costs. Faster output.

But you don’t become a great strategist by learning how to write better prompts.

You become one by launching campaigns, making mistakes, analysing results, working with clients and learning why things succeed or fail.

That takes time.

You cannot prompt your way into five years of strategic judgment.

And if companies stop giving junior talent the opportunity to develop that judgment, they’ll eventually face a shortage of the very expertise they’re relying on today.

For young marketers entering the industry, this creates an uncomfortable reality:

You can no longer assume a company will give you your first opportunity to learn on a silver platter.

So my advice is to start building experience yourself.

→ Run your own experiments, even with tiny budgets. Do it in public, post what you’re working on even if you’re unemployed officially. 

→ Help small businesses or founders with real marketing challenges. Build proof of what you can do before someone gives you the job title.

→ Learn to use AI, but focus on understanding the decisions behind the work.

→ Find a mentor. Learn from their experience, let them guide you and nurture a close relationship to them so that you’re the first person they recommend in their network. 

I don’t think companies will fully stop investing in junior talent but I do see them hiring less of them and not offering long term contracts after internships. 

But I also wouldn’t advise young marketers to wait around for someone to invest in them.

The next generation of great marketers still needs somewhere to learn.

And companies that forget this might eventually find themselves with plenty of AI tools, but very few people who know how to use them well.

Hiring isn't slowing; it's getting more selective!

Last week I met a founder building an AI-powered recruitment platform, and we talked about where IT hiring is headed. A few things stayed with me:
• Budgets are tighter; clients want engineers productive in week one, not month three.
• Full-time hiring is on hold at many companies; work is moving to contract and dedicated-team models.
• AI skills come up in every conversation, but clients pay for full-stack, platform, and DevOps work with AI built in.

We agreed trust matters more than the number of CVs you send. At LN Webworks, we ensure trust with:
1. Engineers on our own payroll, not freelancers
2. Delivery leads backing every deployment
3. Single engineers or full pods (dev + QA + lead)
4. Predictable pricing for our partners

If you're a tech leader or agency scaling delivery without adding permanent headcount, let's talk!

Ask an AI agent, “How much revenue did we close this month?”

Does it count signed contracts, invoices raised, or money collected?

That distinction can change a hiring decision.

On 18 November, Workday announced plans to acquire Honeydew, which helps AI agents and analytics tools use consistent business definitions. 

The acquisition has not closed yet.

It sounds technical. The commercial implication is straightforward.

Connecting AI to a company’s data doesn’t automatically give it an understanding of how that company operates.

Take a sales team.

An opportunity marked “won” could mean the contract is signed. Finance might still be waiting for the first payment. Delivery might be waiting for the scope to be approved.

Now ask an agent to forecast revenue or recommend where to allocate resources.

Which version of “won” should it use?

My reading of this acquisition: the definitions behind the answer are becoming a valuable part of enterprise software.

For those of us selling software and building GTM systems, that changes discovery.

Before proposing another automated workflow, ask:
“What exactly must happen before an opportunity counts as qualified?”
“Who owns that definition?”
“What decision will someone make using this number?”

Those questions belong in the sales conversation. They determine what the implementation needs to deliver.

A faster workflow built around an ambiguous definition can make the wrong decision happen sooner.

Before automating a revenue process, make sure the business agrees on what its numbers mean.

VERMONT IS EXPENSIVE. SO IS DOING THE SAME WORK TWICE.

The cost of doing business here keeps climbing. Vermont’s small-group health insurance rates are set to rise again in 2027. Hiring is tough in a state where unemployment was 2.6% in September 2026 and the labor force was about 9,500 people smaller than a year earlier.

Nearly one in four Vermonters is 65 or older. When experienced workers retire, employers have to replace their skills as well as fill their jobs. If one person knows how to resolve every billing exception, that knowledge can walk out the door with them.

Start by getting back the hours you’re already paying for.

2. FIX THE CONSTRAINTS.

In Step 1, I used a Vermont contractor example to show how I trace a job from intake to payment. Now imagine three people have reviewed the billing packet and it still goes back. The approved price for extra work is in an email. The job record shows the original amount.

A fourth reviewer still has to chase down the price.

I compare how much work arrives, how much gets through correctly, and where the rest waits. When the same issue slows down job after job, I change how the work gets done.

• Give the next move to one owner. Name who can release routine work, who handles exceptions, and when to escalate. Name a backup so the queue keeps moving when someone is out.
• Fix the data at the source. Put the approved scope and price on the job record when the change is approved. Give billing access to that record.
• Make every approval earn its place. Ask what risk the check controls and what evidence the reviewer needs. Keep necessary controls. Remove duplicate checks when one adequately covers the risk.
• Write down the decision. Billing can release an invoice when completed work and approved charges match the contract and change orders. A dispute, mismatch, or missing sign-off goes to a named decision-maker. Test the rule against real cases.

Measure what the business gets back.

Track first-pass quality, completions per week, and the age of open work. Put recovered hours to work serving paying customers or avoiding overtime. That’s how capacity can help protect margins as costs rise. Track from job completion to invoice and from invoice to payment so you can see whether cash actually came in sooner.

I’ve been saying this for years. STABILIZE. STANDARDIZE. OPTIMIZE. Once the workflow is reliable, AI can flag missing documents or pull details from a change order. Count the time spent reviewing and correcting its output. Then compare the financial benefit with what it costs to implement and run.

What could your team get done this week if it spent less time fixing work it already did? If a recurring bottleneck is holding up delivery or billing, message me.

The talent landscape is evolving. But are organisations evolving their approach to hiring at the same pace?

One thing that stands out when looking at today's hiring market is that the challenge is no longer just about finding candidates. It's about identifying the right capabilities.

A few shifts are worth paying attention to:

• Skills over titles: A job title doesn't always reflect someone's true capabilities. Transferable skills and practical experience are becoming increasingly important.

• AI alongside human intelligence: Automation is making recruitment processes faster, but the ability to assess, understand and connect with the right talent remains valuable.

• Workforce planning beyond immediate vacancies: Businesses need to anticipate future skill requirements rather than react only when a position becomes vacant.

• Flexible talent models: Permanent, contract and project-based hiring are increasingly becoming part of the same workforce strategy.

Here's a statistic worth thinking about: According to CIPD's 2026 Resourcing and Talent Planning report, 58% of UK employers experienced an increase in unsuitable applications, while only 33% saw an increase in suitable applications.

That raises an important question:

Are organisations struggling to find talent, or are they still looking for talent in ways that no longer reflect what their business needs?

I believe the future of talent acquisition will be shaped not just by how quickly organisations hire, but by how effectively they understand, identify and engage the capabilities their business needs.

The conversation needs to move beyond filling positions to building the right workforce for what comes next.

Enterprises are getting more serious about measuring the ROI of their AI investments. And that's creating a new challenge for AI vendors because better ROI measurement could expose just how poorly substantiated their value claims are.
 
Nebuly just raised a $21M Series A led by Planven to measure what enterprise AI agents are worth. Its customers include Oura, Iveco Group, CNH and Zeiss, and contracts typically start around $100,000 a year. Their platform breaks work into tasks and estimates the hours AI saves, and Nebuly says its assumptions are visible and configurable.
 
That’s a serious, useful product. Boards are starting to ask what AI is worth, and someone has to answer with more than adoption charts.
 
But, the uncomfortable consequence for AI vendors is that once your buyer’s finance team has a tool that shows the assumptions behind an ROI figure, they’ll start expecting the same from you. A case study that says “saved 20,000 hours” will look thin next to a dashboard that shows how hours were counted, what the baseline was, and which assumptions were changed.
 
Basically, measurement raises the bar for evidence. And hours saved are not dollars saved. A task that drops from three hours to 15 minutes frees time. Whether that time becomes budget, output or nothing depends on what the team does with it. That’s a mechanism question, and it’s exactly what a strong customer story explains.
 
"Our agent saved a support team $2M" will no longer be good enough to convince buyers, when you need to be saying, "Our agent took over password resets and order lookups. Our customer kept headcount flat while ticket volume grew [X]% over nine months. Their finance team counts the value as hiring avoided, not cost cut.” 
 
The second version states the mechanism, the time period and how the customer itself valued it. A CFO can argue with it, which is exactly why they’ll trust it.
 
Are your customers’ finance teams recalculating your ROI claims yet? Whether the answer is yes/no, you need to be prepared with better case studies.

From Blank Floor to 24/7 Live AI Infrastructure: How We Built a Mission-Critical Operation from Scratch: Walking onto an empty white space with a mandate to build a live, 24/7 AI data center operation is both thrilling and daunting. I had the privilege of leading this exact journey from zero to full production, overseeing the transition from deployment to operation, the end-to-end installation and deployment of high-density NVIDIA GB300 GPU clusters powered by direct-to-chip liquid cooling.
Looking back, turning an ambitious blueprint into a relentless 24/7 operation came down to building on five core pillars, step by step. Behind each one enough to fill an entire book and still barely scratch the surface.

1. Starting with People & Leadership
Starting from scratch meant hiring, mentoring, and motivating a brand-new 24/7 technical team. To turn individual engineers into a cohesive unit, I built a multi-layered training ecosystem: intensive 1-on-1 coaching, peer-to-peer knowledge sharing, and specialized vendor-led sessions. We drilled SOPs and live troubleshooting scenarios until calm, methodical execution under pressure became second nature.

2. Mastering the Technology
installation, rigorous testing, validation, and deep troubleshooting. Balancing extreme thermal dynamics and fluid mechanics alongside massive compute loads 

3. Building Operational Frameworks
To protect the facility against the unexpected, we wrote the playbook from the ground up. We established crystal-clear Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) detailing the exact steps to follow during an outage, and we ran live drills to build real muscle memory. At the same time, we implemented strict physical and operational security frameworks and mapped out a critical spare parts inventory, ensuring that if a component failed at 3:00 AM, the exact replacement was already on the shelf.

4. Aligning Vendors & Customers
No mission-critical operation thrives in isolation. As we transitioned from deployment to live operations, we managed vendor and customer relationships side by side. When complex issues arose, close vendor partnerships helped us cut through red tape for rapid root-cause resolution. Simultaneously, enforcing strict SLAs and maintaining transparent communication gave our customers complete confidence that their workloads were in safe hands.

5. Financial 
Finally, world-class engineering only succeeds when it is financially sustainable. Throughout the build and daily operations, we governed every initiative within strict CapEx and OpEx frameworks, holding full P&L accountability. Whether forecasting critical spares, negotiating vendor contracts, or optimizing 24/7 shift coverage, every decision was weighed to maximize uptime while protecting the bottom line.

A few small changes to your CV could make it easier to find you — and see what you can offer.
Here are six practical tips for anyone updating theirs:

1️⃣ Make it easy to contact you
Include your email and phone number, and check they’re correct.
I’ve just placed a candidate whose number was one digit short on their CV. Luckily, I guessed they’d missed the ‘7’ after +44. You don’t want your next opportunity relying on guesswork!

2️⃣ Include where you’re based
A postcode area is enough; you don’t need your full address. It helps people assess whether the commute is realistic. If you’re open to relocating, mention that too.

3️⃣ Put your most recent experience first
Start with your current or most recent role and work backwards. Make it easy to find your recent responsibilities and relevant experience.

4️⃣ My personal opinion: your CV doesn’t need to fit on one page
Unless stated otherwise, I’d rather see relevant detail than lose useful experience to meet a page limit.

Recruiters often search CVs for specific skills, systems, qualifications and industries. If you’ve done it but haven’t mentioned it, you could miss out on appearing in a search.

Name your industries, too. Listing an automotive employer doesn’t guarantee the word “automotive” appears on your CV. Recruiters won’t know every business in every sector, so spelling it out helps you get found.

5️⃣ Explain shorter periods of employment
If a role was a contract, maternity cover or ended through redundancy, add a brief note.
Hiring managers often question repeated short stays. “12-month contract” or “role ended due to redundancy” gives helpful context before assumptions are made.

6️⃣ Check your spelling and grammar
I appreciate this isn’t everyone’s strong point, but avoidable mistakes can give the impression you haven’t taken care over your application.

Read it through, use AI to help check it, or ask someone else to proofread it. If you use AI, check that any changes still accurately reflect your experience.

We analysed 100 software and consultancy formal verification vacancies across the UK and USA to see what mid-tier firms and startups are hiring for outside hardware and Big Tech.

WHAT FIRMS WANT FORMAL VERIFICATION FOR

Checking AI-generated code: AI startups hire formal engineers to prove code written by AI agents is safe and bug-free before shipping.

Securing financial protocols: Web3 audit firms and cryptography startups use proofs to ensure decentralised finance protocols and zero-knowledge circuits cannot be exploited.

Validating trading and backend systems: Trading firms and cloud startups build formal tools to verify algorithms, distributed protocols, and compilers.

Certifying safety-critical software: Consultancies and defence contractors prove code meets strict safety rules (like DO-178C for aviation) without relying only on manual testing.

KEY SKILLS EMPLOYERS WANT

Proof tools: Lean 4 leads newer AI and software roles, followed by Coq (Rocq), Isabelle, and SMT solvers like Z3. Dafny, Verus, TLA+, and Certora Prover also appear regularly.

Languages: Rust, C++, Python, and OCaml lead for verification tools and verified systems, plus Solidity for smart contracts and SPARK/Ada for defence.

Core skills: Program logics (separation logic), type systems, static analysis, model checking, and turning plain-English specs into mathematical rules.

Background: Most roles seek mid-to-senior engineers. A PhD in computer science, maths, or logic is often preferred, though strong open-source proof work can substitute.

WHO IS HIRING

AI verification startups (Harmonic, Axiom, Reasonable AI, Zeroth Research, &Truth Software, Alignerr).

Specialist R&D consultancies (Galois, Runtime Verification, Kestrel, GrammaTech, AdaCore).

Web3 audit firms (Certora, Veridise, Trail of Bits, OpenZeppelin, Nethermind, Spearbit).

Trading firms and aerospace/defence consultancies (Jane Street, Expleo, Crown Innovations, Varda Space).

UK VS. THE USA

Market focus: UK roles (London, Cambridge, Oxford, Bristol) lean toward AI startups, quant finance, and defence consultancies. US roles include more VC-backed AI startups, R&D labs, and remote Web3 audit firms.

Remote work: About half of US roles and a third of UK roles are fully remote; London startups and UK defence firms favour hybrid work.

Pay: US base salaries run $140k to $300k+ ($80 to $200/hr for remote Lean 4 contracts). UK defence pay is £45k to £75k; London AI startups and Web3 audit firms pay £85k to £200k+ (up to £320k+ for senior auditors).

METHODOLOGY AND LIMITS 

We reviewed 100 live roles across the USA (62) and UK (38), excluding chipmakers, hardware firms, and mega-corporations. Because software verification is a smaller niche than chip testing, this sample includes dedicated formal engineers alongside security, AI, and safety-critical roles where mathematical proof is a core duty. Research was performed by AI, so 100% accuracy cannot be guaranteed.

Naked Truth: De ce nu mai participăm la (toate) licitațiile? 🤷‍♀️

Din experiența noastră, am învățat că nu orice oportunitate merită automat toate resursele, timpul și energia pe care suntem tentați să le investim.

Licitațiile pot implica săptămâni sau luni de muncă, strategie și mobilizarea mai multor oameni. Iar uneori, raportul dintre efort și rezultat ridică întrebări importante.

1. Investiția de resurse nu vine întotdeauna cu transparență și feedback.

Poți petrece luni pregătind documentații, adaptând soluții și construind o ofertă competitivă, pentru ca procesul să se oprească fără feedback. Nu afli ce nu a funcționat, unde ai pierdut puncte sau ce a făcut diferența.

Înțelegem că feedbackul detaliat nu este întotdeauna posibil, dar în parteneriatele B2B transparența și comunicarea ar trebui să fie parte dintr-o relație profesională sănătoasă.

2. Unde se termină evaluarea competențelor și unde începe exploatarea ideilor?

O licitație presupune adesea mai mult decât o ofertă financiară. Înseamnă strategie, brainstorming, soluții personalizate și idei dezvoltate special pentru nevoile clientului.

Practic, pui pe masă o parte din expertiza și know-how-ul echipei tale. Problema apare când acestea sunt analizate și valorificate, fără ca furnizorul care le-a dezvoltat să ajungă să le implementeze.

Nu orice idee devine automat proprietatea celui care o formulează, dar timpul și munca intelectuală a participanților merită tratate cu responsabilitate profesională.

True story 

În urmă cu 3 ani, am câștigat o licitație pentru recrutarea a minimum 50 de poziții IT & Engineering. Procesul de licitație a durat peste 6 luni, iar negocierea contractului încă 4. În total, 10 luni de efort și resurse investite, o miză importantă, mai ales pentru un start-up.

Deși contractul avea o durată de 3 ani, am încercat în repetate rânduri să inițiem o discuție cu departamentul HR, să înțelegem hiring plan-ul, prioritățile și cum puteam deveni un sprijin real.

Răspunsurile primite au fost dezinteresate, uneori chiar agresive, iar insistența de a solicita o întâlnire a fost interpretată drept lipsă de respect.

Deznodământul? În 3 ani, FlexibleHR nu a primit nici măcar o poziție în lucru. O singură întâlnire cu HR, obținută cu greu, ne-a clarificat că nu exista o intenție reală de colaborare.

Efort și implicare 100%. Rezultat: ZERO.

Sigur, contractul nu obliga clientul la un anumit volum de recrutări și nu presupunea exclusivitate. Dar dincolo de documentele semnate, un parteneriat presupune intenție reală, comunicare și deschidere reciprocă.

LESSON LEARNED: Un contract câștigat nu garantează un parteneriat.

Nu orice contract merită câștigat cu orice preț și nu orice oportunitate este, în realitate, o oportunitate de business.

Te-ai regăsit într-o astfel de situație? Cum ai reacționat? Feedbackul comunității noastre ne ajută să învățăm și să facem mai bine. 🙏

Karnataka will teach artificial intelligence to Class 9 students in eighteen hundred government high schools this academic year.

Python. Computer vision. Natural language processing. Topics many of us first met in college are now going into a Class 9 timetable.

I think this is the right direction. A child in a government school deserves the same early start as a child in an expensive private school. AI will be part of almost every job these students apply for.

But one line in the news stayed with me. The department has started hiring guest teachers to deliver the course.

Guest teachers are often the most stretched people in a school. Short contracts, long commutes, very little time for their own training. Now we are asking them to teach a subject that changes every few months.

A curriculum is only as strong as the teacher standing in front of the class. Not the syllabus. The support.

If this is going to work, teachers need three things before students do. Real training, with time set aside for it. A small circle of other AI teachers they can call when a lesson goes wrong. And tools that take routine checking off their desk, so their hours go into explaining, not marking.

Karnataka has taken the first step. The second step is the teacher.

Teachers and school leaders, if your school started teaching AI next term, what support would your teachers need first?

If you're hiring a creative strategist right now, you're not competing with other brands. You're competing with the freelance market.
⠀
Last year I got around 50 offers. Most were full-time, one brand, $4-6K a month on average. It doesn't make sense if you can work with a few brands and make over $15K.
⠀
Here's the paradox I keep seeing in job descriptions.
⠀
Brands want a strategist who owns everything. Runs the research and analysis. Briefs and manages the team. Controls the process. Knows AI generation and automation tools. Jumps into an overloaded brand workflow and gets it moving fast. Doesn't need direction at every step.
⠀
But think about what's going on in the head of someone who can actually do all that. If they don't need managing, they can run this for three or four brands at once. With their own workflow and no extra layers of approvals, they spend less time on ops and more on what moves performance.
⠀
That person is rarely looking to be tied to one brand.
⠀
Partly it's just insurance. Lose one contract and the other two still pay the bills. Tie yourself to one brand, and if something goes wrong there, often nothing to do with creative strategy, you lose everything overnight.
⠀
The market is starting to adjust. I'm seeing more offers built as a $4-8K base plus a percentage tied to results. Some brands now agree to part-time, retainer or contract work. Still a minority. Most still want full-time.
⠀
And there's a bonus most brands miss. A strategist working across several brands brings in what's working in other niches: hooks, formats, angles. A strategist inside one brand only ever sees one account.
⠀
I've done this many times. You spot an early winner in one niche, an angle nobody in the other niches has used yet, bring it to another brand you work with, and it becomes a winner there too.
⠀
If you need someone fully independent, hire them the way independent people want to work. Tie it to performance, that's fair. Just don't make full-time the only option.
⠀
And I'm 200% sure of this: if you turn out to be a good fit for each other, that person will happily consider a full-time role on terms that work for both sides.
⠀
Founders, CMOs and HR: how are you structuring creative strategy hires right now?
⠀
Creative strategists: are you full-time, or on contract and retainer?
⠀
